title: Git bisect for regression investigation
description: Learn about Git bisect for regression investigation. Master the concepts, patterns, and best practices.

data.text: Git bisect uses binary search to pinpoint the exact commit that introduced a regression. Instead of checking out every commit manually, bisect narrows the search space exponentially, turning a hours-long investigation into minutes.

data.title: Lesson Scope
data.text: This lesson covers manual bisect, automated bisect with shell scripts, handling merge commits, and integrating bisect into CI.
How Binary Search Works in Git
Binary search is a divide-and-conquer strategy. Git checks out a middle commit, you mark it as good or bad, and the search space halves. After log2(N) steps, the first bad commit is identified.

data.title: Binary Search Analogy
data.code: Imagine a book with 1,000 pages. You do not read every page. You open to the middle, decide if the answer is before or after that page, and repeat. Git bisect does the same with commits.

data.text: Starting a Bisect Session
Before starting, you need two references: a known good commit and a known bad commit. Git uses these anchors to define the search range.

data.title: Starting Bisect
data.code:
git bisect start

git bisect bad HEAD

git bisect good v2.3.0

# Git now checks out a middle commit

data.title: Finding Good and Bad Commits
data.text: Use git log, git tag, or git describe to locate approximate good and bad commits. The more accurate the anchors, the faster bisect converges.
Marking Commits During Bisect
After Git checks out a middle commit, test it. If the regression is present, mark it bad. If the code works, mark it good.

data.title: Marking Commits
data.code:
# Test the current checkout...

# If the bug is present
git bisect bad

# If the bug is not present
git bisect good

data.text: Bisect Output
When the search finishes, Git reports the first bad commit, its hash, author, date, and message. You can immediately inspect the diff with git show.

data.title: Bisect Result
data.code:
# When the search converges, Git prints the culprit. You are still
# in bisect mode, so run 'git bisect reset' when you are done:

abc1234 is the first bad commit
commit abc1234
Author: Jane Doe <jane@example.com>
Date:   Mon Sep 10 14:32:00 2026

    fix(parser): optimize regex for edge cases

    Introduces a regression when parsing nested arrays.

# Inspect the offending change
git show abc1234

data.text: Resetting After Bisect
Always end a bisect session by returning to your original branch. Git bisect reset checks out the branch you were on before starting bisect and removes the temporary bisect state.

data.title: Resetting Bisect
data.code: git bisect reset

data.title: Do Not Forget to Reset
data.text: Leaving a bisect session active can confuse teammates who see an unexpected detached HEAD in the repository.
Automated Bisect
If you can write a script that exits 0 when the code is good and 1 when it is bad, Git can run bisect automatically. This is the fastest way to hunt regressions.

data.title: Automated Bisect Script
Running Automated Bisect
data.code:
git bisect start HEAD v2.3.0

git bisect run ./test.sh

# Git runs test.sh at each step and decides good or bad automatically

data.title: Script Exit Codes Matter
data.text: Git interprets exit code 0 as good, 125 as skip, and anything else as bad. Make sure your test script follows this contract exactly.
Skipping Commits
Some commits are untestable or irrelevant, such as massive formatting commits. Mark them with git bisect skip, and Git will ignore them in the binary search.

data.title: Skipping a Commit
data.code: git bisect skip abc1234

data.text: Bisect with Merge Commits
By default, Git bisect treats merge commits as untestable and skips them. Use the --first-parent option if you want to trace regressions along the main integration branch only.

data.title: Bisecting Along First Parent
data.code: git bisect start --first-parent HEAD v2.3.0

data.text: Using git bisect visualize
git bisect visualize opens a pager with the log of commits in the current bisect range. This helps you understand which commits remain under evaluation.

data.title: Visualize Bisect Range
data.code: git bisect visualize

data.text: Bisect Log and Replay
You can record a bisect session with git bisect log and replay it later or share it with teammates. This is useful for documenting how a regression was tracked down.

data.title: Logging and Replaying Bisect
data.code:
# Save the bisect session
git bisect log > bisect.log

# Replay on another clone
git bisect replay bisect.log

data.text: Automated Regression Detection in CI
Some teams run bisect automatically in CI when a regression is detected on main. The CI system finds the first bad commit and comments on the pull request with the culprit.

data.title: CI Bisect Comment
data.code:
## Regression Detected

Automated bisect identified abc1234 as the first bad commit:

"fix(parser): optimize regex for edge cases"

Please review this change for the regression.

data.text: Common Bisect Pitfalls

items: Starting bisect from a dirty working tree
Using incorrect good or bad anchors
Forgetting to skip untestable commits
Running bisect on a shallow clone with insufficient history
Leaving the repository in a detached HEAD state after finishing

data.title: Shallow Clones and Bisect
data.text: If you cloned with --depth, bisect may fail because the needed commits are missing. Fetch full history before bisecting with git fetch --unshallow.
Handling Flaky Tests

Flaky tests break automated bisect because a test may pass on one commit and fail on the next for unrelated reasons. Stabilize tests first, or modify the script to run the test multiple times and require consistent results.

data.title: Flaky-Test-Aware Script
data.code:
#!/bin/bash
pass=0
fail=0
for i in 1 2 3; do
  if npm test -- --grep "regression-test"; then
    pass=$((pass+1))
  else
    fail=$((fail+1))
  fi
done
[ $pass -gt $fail ] && exit 0 || exit 1

data.text: Bisect and Binary Search Complexity

Bisect takes O(log N) steps where N is the number of commits in the range. For a history of 1,000 commits, that is about 10 steps. For 1,000,000 commits, it is about 20 steps. The efficiency gain over linear search is enormous.
Alternatives to Bisect

Sometimes a simple git log -S or git log -G search is enough. These commands find commits that added or removed a specific string or pattern, which can quickly surface a suspicious commit without bisect.

data.title: Finding Commits That Changed a String
data.code:
git log -S "parseArray" --oneline

git log -G "nested.*array" --oneline

data.title: Combine Tools
data.text: Use git log -S first to narrow suspects, then run bisect on the smaller candidate range for faster results.
Documenting the Finding
After bisect identifies the culprit, document the finding in your issue tracker. Include the commit hash, author, why it introduced the regression, and the fix.

data.title: Issue Comment Template
data.code:
Root cause: commit abc1234 by Jane Doe.

Change: optimized regex for edge cases.
Regression: nested arrays fail to parse when they contain comments.
Fix: revert regex or add comment-aware tokenizer.

data.text: Advanced Bisect Techniques
These techniques cover the practical edge cases of bisect: build steps, worktrees, merge commits, and notebooks.
Prerequisites for Bisect
Before starting bisect, you need a reproducible regression, a known good commit, and a known bad commit. Without these, bisect cannot function.

items: A reliable way to test whether the bug is present
A commit hash where the bug does not exist
A commit hash where the bug does exist, usually HEAD
Sufficient history between the two commits

data.text: Starting Bisect with Good and Bad Anchors
You can specify good and bad in any order. Git automatically determines the search range and begins checking out commits between the two anchors.

data.title: Starting Bisect with Tag
data.code:
git bisect start

git bisect bad HEAD

git bisect good v2.3.0

data.text: Bisect with Dates
If you know approximately when the regression was introduced, you can use git log --before and --after to find candidate commits, then use those as bisect anchors.

data.title: Finding Commits by Date
data.code: git log --oneline --before='2026-09-01' --after='2026-08-15'

data.text: Bisect View
The git bisect view command shows the remaining range of commits under evaluation. This helps you understand how much of the search space is left.

data.title: Viewing Bisect Range
data.code: git bisect visualize --oneline

data.text: Bisect Skip Reasons
You may need to skip commits that are untestable, missing build artifacts, or part of a massive reformatting. Skipping too many commits reduces bisect accuracy.

items: Commit removed the test infrastructure
Commit is a formatting-only change
Build is broken and cannot be tested
Commit is a merge commit with untestable changes

data.text: Writing Robust Test Scripts
An automated bisect script should be deterministic, fast, and independent of environment state. Avoid network calls, time-dependent assertions, and external dependencies in test scripts.

items: Use local mocks instead of external APIs
Avoid sleep or timeout-based assertions
Reset the database to a known state before each test
Log output for debugging failed bisect runs

data.text: Bisect with Build Steps
If your test requires a build step, include it in the bisect script. Git runs the script at every step, so the script must handle checking out, building, and testing.

data.title: Bisect Script with Build
data.code:
#!/bin/bash
npm install
npm run build
npm test -- --grep "regression-test"

data.text: Bisecting Across Multiple Branches
If the regression could have been introduced on any of several branches, bisect each branch separately. Use --first-parent to trace along the main integration branch.

data.title: Bisecting Along First Parent
data.code: git bisect start --first-parent HEAD origin/main~50

data.text: Bisect with Git Worktrees
Git worktrees let you run multiple bisect sessions simultaneously without checking out different commits in the same working directory. This is useful when investigating multiple regressions at once.

data.title: Creating a Worktree for Bisect
data.code:
git worktree add /tmp/bisect-worktree HEAD
git bisect -C /tmp/bisect-worktree start HEAD v2.3.0

data.text: Bisect and Merge Conflicts
If a commit in the bisect range has a merge conflict, the automated script may fail. You can either skip the commit or write a script that resolves trivial conflicts automatically.

data.title: Skipping Merge Commits
data.code: git bisect skip $(git rev-list --merges HEAD..v2.3.0)

data.text: Bisect Log Analysis
After bisect finishes, review the bisect log to understand the search path. This can reveal whether the regression was introduced in a straightforward commit or required skipping many commits.

data.title: Analyzing Bisect Log
data.code:
git bisect log | wc -l

# Shows how many steps bisect took

data.text: Bisect in Jupyter or Notebook Environments

For data science or notebook-based regressions, write a bisect script that runs a specific notebook cell or script and checks the output. This bisects regressions in analysis pipelines, not just application code.

data.title: Bisecting a Notebook Regression

data.text: Preserving Bisect Results

Document bisect results in your issue tracker. Include the commit hash, author, date, and a brief explanation of the regression. Future teams can use this information to improve testing and code review.

data.title: Bisect Documentation Template
data.code:
## Regression Investigation: #511

### First Bad Commit
abc1234 by Jane Doe on 2026-09-10

### Root Cause
The commit optimized a regex for edge cases but broke nested array parsing.

### Remediation
Revert the regex change or add a comment-aware tokenizer.

### Prevention
Add a regression test for nested arrays with comments.

data.text: Common Bisect Errors

items: fatal: not a git repository - run bisect inside a valid repo
bad/food anchor not a commit - verify the anchor is a valid SHA or ref
fatal: ambiguous argument - the ref does not exist; check spelling
Automatic merge failed - the script produced a conflict; skip or fix the script

data.text: Bisect Performance
Bisect performance depends on test script speed. If each test takes 30 seconds, 20 bisect steps take 10 minutes. Optimize tests to run in seconds, not minutes.

items: Use unit tests instead of E2E tests when possible
Mock external dependencies
Run only the relevant test suite, not the entire suite
Use test parallelization if available

data.text: When Bisect Is Not the Right Tool

Bisect requires a reproducible regression. If the bug is intermittent, environment-dependent, or requires complex manual steps, bisect will produce unreliable results. Use other debugging techniques first.

items: Bug is flaky or non-deterministic
Bug requires manual UI interaction to reproduce
Bug depends on external system state
Bug was introduced gradually across many commits

data.text: Summary

Git bisect is one of the most powerful debugging tools in a senior engineer's arsenal. Combined with automated test scripts, it turns regressions into a repeatable, fast, and reliable investigation process.

data.title: Key Takeaways
text: Use git bisect start with good and bad anchors
Prefer automated bisect with a test script
Reset with git bisect reset when finished
Use git log -S to narrow suspects before bisecting
